title: Uncertainty-aware auto-segmentation enables adaptive radiotherapy planning of liver metastases.
abstract: Purpose Despite remarkable auto-segmentation performance and growing clinical adoption, models frequently fail to generalize beyond the training distribution. Therefore, this study aimed to develop and validate an uncertainty-aware segmentation pipeline that yields high delineation accuracy for liver cancer patients and reliably identifies safety-critical segmentation imperfections in radiotherapy. Materials and methods Datasets of n = 173 patients with 224 liver metastases were divided into training (n = 100), validation (n = 33), and test (n = 40). Each case included annotated T2-weighted magnetic resonance images. An nnU-Net segmented treatment-relevant organs and provided a margin-extended hepatic mask, which served as input to a second-stage SE-ResUNet for lesion delineation. Uncertainty was approximated via checkpoint ensembling under a cyclic learning-rate schedule, yielding entropy-based uncertainty maps and case-wise uncertainty scores. These guided an adaptive post-inference analysis consisting of (i) detection of potentially missed lesions and (ii) identification of problematic contours. Performance was evaluated on 40 patients (n = 52 lesions) using Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC), 95%-Hausdorff-Distance (HD95), expected calibration error (ECE), uncertainty coverage, and the correlation between case-wise uncertainty scores and segmentation accuracy. Results Overall performance across treatment-relevant organs was DSC/HD95 = 0.89/4.8 mm; lesionsegmentation achieved DSC/HD95 = 0.86/4.9 mm. Uncertainty-guided post-processing, triggered in 14/40 cases, recovered 7 initially missed metastases, increasing lesion-level sensitivity from 84.6% (44/52) to 98.1% (51/52). Uncertainty estimates showed good calibration with ECE/uncertainty coverage for organs/lesion of 7.2/93.7% and 7.5/98.3%, and significant correlation between uncertainty/DSC (r = -0.802). Conclusion The proposed pipeline seamlessly integrates accurate organ/lesion segmentation, interpretable uncertainty, and anatomy-guided post-processing to detect safety-critical segmentation failures and enable trustworthy AI auto-segmentation in clinical routine.

title: Classification of Vertebral Artery Course Variations in the Atlantoaxial Region and Their Anatomic Considerations for Surgical Planning: A CTA Imaging Analysis of 511 Patients.
abstract: Background Vertebral artery (VA) course variations in the atlantoaxial region pose significant risks during posterior C1-C2 fixation. This study aimed to classify these variations on CT angiography (CTA) and assess their anatomic implications for surgical planning. Methods A retrospective analysis was conducted on 511 patients (1,022 vertebral arteries) who underwent cervical CTA at Beijing Tongren Hospital between January 2019 and December 2024. Vertebral artery course variations were classified by two independent senior radiologists. Interobserver agreement was assessed using Cohen's kappa coefficient. Associations between variation types and gender/side were analyzed using chi-square tests with adjusted standardized residuals. potential surgical implications were assessed based on anatomical relationships and literature review Results: Seven types were identified: normal type (712 arteries, 70%), high-riding type (243, 24%), posterior arch bridge type (26, 2.5%), protruding type (14, 1.4%), segmental artery type (13, 1.2%), fenestration type (9, 0.9%), and combined type (5, 0.5%). Interobserver agreement was substantial (κ = 0.795). Each type carries distinct anatomic considerations for screw placement, exposure, and surgical approach selection. Conclusions Different vertebral artery course variation types carry distinct and predictable potential surgical implications. Detailed preoperative CTA assessment with three-dimensional reconstruction is essential for identifying these variations and minimizing the risk of iatrogenic vertebral artery injury during posterior atlantoaxial surgery.

title: Ultrasound renal denervation for treatment-resistant hypertension with severe left ventricular hypertrophy.
abstract: Resistant hypertension with left ventricular hypertrophy requires aggressive treatment to reduce cardiovascular risk. Ultrasound renal denervation safely attenuates sympathetic activity and lowers blood pressure. We performed step-by-step image-guided renal denervation, demonstrating procedural feasibility, safety, and early blood pressure reduction with potential benefits for left ventricular remodeling.

title: Preparation and evaluation of degradable imaging drug loaded embolization microspheres for hepatocellular carcinoma.
abstract: Transarterial chemoembolization (TACE) necessitates the use of embolic agents with intrinsic radiopacity and controlled biodegradability to enhance therapeutic precision. In addressing the limitations inherent in current drug-eluting microspheres (DEMs), this study introduces the development of inherently radiopaque and biodegradable (DOX+Lipiodol) @PLGA @CaCO 3 @Alg core-shell microspheres. These microspheres were synthesized using rotating membrane emulsification and surface-induced ion crosslinking, with calcium carbonate serving multiple roles: a solid surfactant for Pickering stabilization, an acid-neutralizing agent, and an alginate shell inducer. The microspheres successfully encapsulated iodine loads, demonstrated by CT values reaching up to 8,000 HU, and contained doxorubicin at 1.53 ± 0.12 wt.%. They exhibited prolonged radiopacity for over 14 days in vivo and showed a pH-responsive drug release pattern, releasing 90% of their payload at pH 5.2 compared to 30% at pH 7.2 over 120 h. The sequential degradation process (alginate → CaCO 3 → PLGA) resulted in greater than 60% mass loss within four months, correlating with a reduction in CT attenuation. In rabbit embolization models, the microspheres achieved effective vascular occlusion and induced ischemic necrosis in ears and kidneys. CT tracking was possible without additional contrast agents, and systemic biosafety was confirmed with cell viability exceeding 90%, hemolysis below 1%, and normal hematological and histological profiles. These findings suggest that the microspheres could serve as a clinically translatable platform for image-guided TACE, integrating occlusion, therapy, and monitoring into a cohesive treatment strategy.

title: Robot-assisted total laparoscopic pancreaticoduodenectomy with transvaginal specimen extraction: a case report.
abstract: Natural orifice specimen extraction surgery reduces incision-related complications and accelerates postoperative recovery while maintaining oncologic safety, whereas the da Vinci robotic surgical system further enhances the precision of minimally invasive procedures. This case report describes a robot-assisted total laparoscopic pancreaticoduodenectomy combined with transvaginal specimen extraction (RPD-TVSE). The patient was a 64-year-old female with moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma of the descending duodenum. The procedure took 350 min, with intraoperative blood loss of 200 mL; no blood transfusion was administered during the perioperative period. The patient was able to ambulate on postoperative day 1, with no adverse events recorded. Histopathology confirmed tumor staging as pT2N0M0, with all surgical margins negative. At 12-month follow-up, no evidence of recurrence was observed. This case demonstrates that RPD-TVSE is technically feasible and yields favorable short-term outcomes, providing a novel minimally invasive surgical option for female patients. However, long-term oncologic safety requires further investigation and validation.

title: Comparative accuracy of imaging modalities for differentiating malignant small testicular masses.
abstract: Objectives To synthesise evidence comparing the diagnostic performance of imaging modalities in differentiating malignant from benign small testicular masses. Patients and methods A Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA)-compliant search of PubMed, Scopus, Cochrane and Web of Science databases up to 6 May 2026 identified 11 studies comprising 707 patients with small testicular masses (predominantly <2 cm) who underwent imaging prior to a histopathological or, where unavailable, a mixed clinical/radiological follow-up reference standard. Diagnostic accuracy measures for six modalities (brightness-mode [B-Mode] ultrasonography [US], colour doppler US [CDUS], contrast-enhanced US [CEUS], magnetic resonance imaging [MRI], strain elastography [SE] and strain ratio [SR]) were synthesised using a Bayesian bivariate hierarchical summary receiver operating characteristic model. Results The CEUS demonstrated the most reliable discriminatory ability with a pooled sensitivity of 91% and pooled specificity of 81%, yielding the highest diagnostic odds ratio of 46. B-Mode US remains a valid screening test with the highest sensitivity of 96% but a specificity of only 39%. CDUS showed a pooled sensitivity of 69% and a specificity of 81%. MRI had a pooled sensitivity of 91% and a specificity of 38%. SE demonstrated a pooled sensitivity of 87% and a specificity of 56%. Finally, SR reported the lowest sensitivity at 74% and a specificity of 50%. CEUS demonstrated significantly higher specificity than B-Mode US (ratio 1.9, 95% posterior interval [PI] 1.2-4.4) and MRI (ratio 1.8, 95% PI 1.0-5.2). Conclusion The CEUS demonstrates the highest combined sensitivity and specificity for differentiating benign from malignant testicular masses, significantly outperforming conventional B-Mode US and MRI in specificity. CEUS represents a compelling decision-making tool to support testis-sparing strategies and reduce unnecessary orchidectomies for indeterminate small testicular masses.

title: The Solitary Functioning Kidney: From Pathophysiology to Long-Term Management.
abstract: Solitary functioning kidney (SFK) is a clinical condition characterized by the presence of a single functioning kidney, arising from either congenital anomalies or acquired causes. It is recognized as an important risk factor for chronic kidney disease (CKD) and, in some patients, for progression to end-stage kidney disease (ESKD). Congenital solitary functioning kidney is commonly associated with renal hypoplasia or dysplasia, genetic abnormalities, and congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract, whereas acquired solitary functioning kidney is often secondary to unilateral nephrectomy for renal tumors, trauma, tuberculosis, severe infection, or living kidney donation. The principal pathophysiological mechanisms underlying the progression from SFK to CKD are compensatory renal hypertrophy and glomerular hyperfiltration in the remnant kidney. Although these adaptive responses may initially maintain renal function, sustained compensation can lead to glomerular injury, proteinuria, tubulointerstitial damage, and renal fibrosis. Early diagnosis relies primarily on imaging modalities, such as ultrasonography and magnetic resonance imaging, together with assessment of renal function and emerging biomarkers, including neutrophil gelatinase-associated lipocalin and cystatin C. Prognostic evaluation of patients with SFK should comprehensively consider etiology, age, compensatory renal growth, associated urinary tract anomalies, comorbidities, and markers of kidney injury. Effective long-term management is essential to prevent or delay progression to CKD and ESKD, with particular emphasis on individualized follow-up, lifestyle modification, blood pressure control, reduction of proteinuria, and avoidance of additional nephrotoxic insults. Previous publications have often addressed pediatric congenital solitary functioning kidney (CSFK), living kidney donors, and disease-related nephrectomy cohorts separately, limiting the translation of heterogeneous evidence into a common clinical approach. This review integrates congenital and acquired SFK across the life course, distinguishes shared markers of established kidney injury from etiology-specific determinants of renal reserve, and proposes an evidence-informed framework for dynamic risk stratification and risk-adapted follow-up and management. This framework is conceptual and requires prospective validation.

title: Surface-extraction MRI of the fetal brain: an improved approach for diagnosing anomalies associated with antenatal absence of the septum pellucidum.
abstract: Introduction Prenatal imaging is crucial for evaluating neurological development in cases of absence of septum pellucidum (ASP), which may be associated with a spectrum of cortical, cerebellar and ocular anomalies and variable neurodevelopmental outcomes. Recent advances in fetal MRI techniques have improved the detection and characterization of subtle brain abnormalities. Case report A pregnant patient was referred to our tertiary centre for targeted neurosonography at 28weeks of gestation, confirming ASP initially considered isolated. Fetal MRI at 33 weeks suspected associated cortical malformations, with unilateral peri-sylvian polymicrogyria and closed lip schizencephaly, but it partially limited by motion artefacts. Subsequent super‑resolution reconstruction (SRR) and cortical surface extraction confirmed the presence of polymicrogyria associated with schizencephaly. Post-MRI neurosonography also confirmed unilateral perisylvian polymicrogyria and schizencephaly. Following multidisciplinary discussion parents opted for termination of pregnancy. Post‑mortem neuropathological examination confirmed the imaging findings, demonstrating polymicrogyria associated with schizencephaly in the right perisylvian region. Conclusion This case highlights the possible added diagnostic value of advanced fetal MRI post‑processing, which enabled precise characterization of cortical abnormalities not confidently identified on conventional imaging. The strong correlation with neuropathological findings supports the potential role of surface‑based analysis in improving diagnostic accuracy and prenatal counselling in cases of ASP.

title: Retinal Microvascular Abnormalities, White Matter Injury, and Cognitive Impairment in Carotid Stenosis or Occlusion.
abstract: Background Severe carotid artery stenosis or occlusion (CASO) is associated with white matter injury and cognitive impairment, but markers of accompanying microvascular dysfunction remain incompletely characterized. We investigated the relationships among retinal microvascular abnormalities on optical coherence tomography angiography, white matter hyperintensities (WMH), and cognitive impairment in severe unilateral CASO. Methods In this multicenter cross-sectional study, 860 participants were included: 566 patients with severe unilateral CASO without acute cerebral infarction and 294 control participants with similar age and sex distributions. All participants underwent multimodal imaging, including automated WMH segmentation on brain magnetic resonance imaging and macular optical coherence tomography angiography. Cognitive function was assessed using the Montreal Cognitive Assessment. Results Compared with controls, patients with CASO showed lower vessel length density across retinal layers and greater WMH burden. Within the group with CASO, the retina ipsilateral to the stenosis showed lower vessel length density and greater vessel dilation, paralleling the greater burden of deep WMH in the ipsilateral hemisphere (all adjusted P <0.05). Retinal microvascular abnormalities and greater WMH burden were both associated with worse concurrent cognitive performance. Adding optical coherence tomography angiography metrics to clinical and WMH-based models provided modest additional discrimination for identifying concurrent cognitive impairment in internal cross-validation, increasing the area under the curve from 0.652 to 0.695 (Δarea under the curve, 0.043 [95% CI, 0.021-0.064]). Conclusions In severe unilateral CASO, retinal microvascular abnormalities were associated with ipsilateral white matter injury and lower cognitive performance. Optical coherence tomography angiographymetrics provided modest complementary discriminatory information beyond conventional clinical variables and WMH for identifying concurrent cognitive impairment, although external validation is required. title: Thoracic Intermuscular Adiposity, Coronary Microvascular Dysfunction, and Prognosis After Cardiac Surgery.
abstract: Background Body mass index is a widely-used yet imprecise measure of adiposity. Thoracic intermuscular adiposity is reported to be related with coronary microvascular dysfunction (CMD), but their prognostic implications after cardiac surgery are not clear. This study aimed to investigate whether computed tomography-derived thoracic intermuscular adiposity and CMD provide better prognostic information than body mass index in patients undergoing cardiac surgery. Methods This study consecutively enrolled 666 patients undergoing elective surgery from 3 centers. Using computed tomography at the T12 vertebral level, we quantified the cross-sectional areas (cm 2 ) of skeletal muscle, subcutaneous adipose tissue, and intermuscular adipose tissue. Intermuscular fat fraction was calculated as intermuscular adipose tissue/(intermuscular adipose tissue+skeletal muscle)×100%. CMD was defined by a coronary angiography-derived index of microcirculatory resistance >25. The primary end point was major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), a composite of all-cause mortality, myocardial infarction, and rehospitalization for heart failure. Results A total of 63 MACEs (9.5%) occurred during a median 17-month follow-up. Obesity defined by body mass index (10.7% of patients) was not associated with MACE ( P =0.187). Each 1% increase in intermuscular fat fraction was significantly associated with CMD (adjusted odds ratio, 1.22 [95% CI, 1.14-1.31]; P <0.001), whereas body mass index showed no such correlation ( P =0.964). CMD independently predicted MACE (adjusted hazard ratio, 2.03; [95% CI: 1.15-3.61]; P = 0.015), whereas intermuscular fat fraction did not ( P =0.516). The annualized MACE rate was significantly higher in patients with CMD (11.0% versus 5.2%, P =0.004). Conclusions Computed tomography-derived intermuscular adiposity correlated strongly with CMD, and preprocedural CMD was associated with a higher risk of MACE after cardiac surgery. External validation and prospective studies are warranted.

title: Delayed Multi-Compartment Traumatic Hernias After Blunt Abdominal Trauma: A Case-Based Review of Diagnosis and Staged Management.
abstract: BackgroundTraumatic diaphragmatic hernias (TDHs) and traumatic abdominal wall hernias (TAWHs) are uncommon sequelae of blunt abdominal trauma (BAT) and may be missed during the initial evaluation. Delayed presentation can occur months to years later, resulting in incarceration, obstruction, or respiratory compromise.Case PresentationA 61-year-old woman presented 1 year after a motor vehicle collision with abdominal pain, nausea, constipation, and dyspnea. Computed tomography demonstrated an incarcerated left diaphragmatic hernia containing colon and omentum, along with a right flank hernia containing ascending colon. Review of prior imaging revealed a flank hematoma and subtle abdominal wall disruption at the time of initial injury. The patient underwent urgent laparoscopic repair of the diaphragmatic hernia followed by elective robotic transabdominal preperitoneal repair of the flank hernia 2 months later.DiscussionThis case illustrates a pattern of delayed multi-compartment traumatic herniation resulting from thoracoabdominal force transmission. Diagnostic delays may occur because of competing priorities during polytrauma management, limitations of initial imaging, and delayed development of herniation, especially when the injuries are subtle. Findings such as rib fractures, pneumothorax, abdominal wall hematoma, and persistent symptoms should prompt continued surveillance.ConclusionDelayed multi-compartment traumatic hernias represent a diagnostic challenge requiring a high index of suspicion, longitudinal surveillance, and individualized management. A staged operative approach based on symptom severity and anatomic location can effectively address differing levels of clinical urgency.

title: Iron oxide nanoparticles for hepatocellular carcinoma theranostics: From nanoplatform design to clinical translation.
abstract: The challenges in early diagnosis and effective treatment of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) are largely attributable to the underlying cirrhosis, impaired hepatic reserve, and the added complexity of heterogeneous tumor vascularity in many patients. Iron oxide nanoparticles (IONPs) are promising platforms for HCC diagnosis and treatment because of their magnetic properties, tunable magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) contrast, magnetothermal conversion capability, and modifiable surface chemistry. These features enable IONPs to be used for image-guided diagnosis, liver-directed locoregional therapy, systemic drug delivery, and treatment monitoring. In this review, we summarize the composition, crystal structure, size-dependent magnetic properties, surface modification, and in vivo fate of IONPs, along with how these characteristics influence their performance in HCC imaging and therapy. For diagnostic applications, we focus on passive accumulation, particularly mononuclear phagocyte system (MPS)-mediated hepatic contrast, ligand-mediated active targeting, and multimodal imaging. We then review therapeutic strategies, including magnetic hyperthermia (MHT), stimuli-responsive drug delivery, and combination therapy. Major barriers to clinical translation are also addressed, encompassing the heterogeneous enhanced permeability and retention (EPR) effect, high background uptake by non-tumoral liver tissue, liver function-related safety concerns, limitations of alternating magnetic fields, and manufacturing reproducibility.

title: AMSSE-SwinTrans: A harmonized multimodal hybrid framework with explainable AI for ischemic stroke lesion segmentation.
abstract: BackgroundAccurate ischemic stroke lesion segmentation from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is important but challenging due to variability in lesion morphology. Traditional convolutional neural networks (CNNs) effectively capture local spatial features but often struggle to capture long-range contextual dependencies needed for irregular lesions. Transformer-based architectures are good at capturing global context; however, they are computationally expensive and difficult to deploy in resource-constrained environments. The black-box nature of deep learning models limits their clinical adoption owing to lack of transparency.ObjectiveThis study introduces AMSSE-SwinTrans, a lightweight hybrid CNN-Transformer framework to make stroke lesion segmentation accurate, efficient and interpretable across different MRI modalities.MethodsThis study proposes AMSSE-SwinTrans, a lightweight hybrid CNN-Transformer framework that combines adaptive multi-scale squeeze-and-excitation (AMSSE) module with simplified transformer blocks employing multi-head self-attention, along with explainable AI (XAI) for clinical interpretation. The model was evaluated on a single-channel harmonized multimodal two-dimensional MRI Slices from ATLAS v2.0 and ISLES 2022 dataset.ResultsThe model achieved an overall Dice of 0.8629, lesion-specific Dice of 0.7535. An ablation study demonstrated a significant performance improvement when each component was added. The model comparisons were all significant with Wilcoxon signed-rank test yielding p-value ( p < 0.001) across all comparisons. With only 27.67 M parameters, 17.67 GFLOPs, and 9.22 ms inference time per slice, the architecture is well-suited for deployment in resource-constrained clinical settings. The interpretability of the model is supported by Attention Rollout and Grad-CAM++ visualizations.ConclusionAMSSE-SwinTrans establishes itself as a resource-efficient and interpretable framework for multimodal stroke lesion segmentation.

title: CT-based 3D morphometric reference data on osseous TMJ subunits in a European cohort: relevance for patient-specific implant research.
abstract: Background Patient-specific alloplastic prostheses are increasingly used for reconstruction of the temporomandibular joint (TMJ). However, the extent to which articulating implant components should reflect native osseous TMJ morphology remains unresolved. This study used CT-derived three-dimensional (3D) virtual-digital surface models to analyze osseous TMJ subunits in humans and provide morphometric reference data for future patient-specific TMJ implant research. Methods In this retrospective exploratory study, 97 computed tomography (CT) scans from Hannover Medical School were analyzed. High-quality 3D virtual-digital models of the articulating TMJ subunits, including the mandibular condyle and glenoid fossa, were generated and used to measure relevant TMJ parameters. Parameters were compared according to sex and age, and correlation analyses were performed. Results Morphometric variability was observed among the osseous TMJ subunits. Men showed larger medial-lateral diameters of the mandibular condyle, greater articular tubercle height, and larger zygomatic arch root dimensions. Women showed a larger anterior-posterior diameter of the glenoid fossa. Middle-aged participants showed a larger anterior-posterior diameter of the mandibular condyle and larger sagittal dimensions of the zygomatic arch root compared with young-aged participants. Correlation analysis revealed associations between selected parameters, particularly between zygomatic arch root diameter and articular tubercle height. Conclusion This study provides CT-based 3D morphometric reference data on osseous TMJ subunits in a European cohort. The findings indicate inter-individual morphometric variability and exploratory sex- and age-related differences in selected parameters. These data may provide anatomical reference information for future patient-specific TMJ implant research. However, the present study does not evaluate implant fit, mandibular kinematics, biomechanical performance, or clinical outcomes. Therefore, the translational relevance of these findings requires further validation.

title: From equilibrium to dynamic metabolic imaging: the evolving role of magnetic resonance spectroscopic imaging in neurodegenerative disorders.
abstract: Background Dysregulated brain metabolism is increasingly recognized to play a significant role in the development and progression of neurodegenerative diseases (NDDs). Conventional imaging methods, such as positron emission tomography (PET), are limited to assessing tracer uptake and offer no insight into its downstream metabolic fate. Additionally, PET provides no insight into dynamic metabolic fluxes and turnover, which reflect biochemical processes. In contrast, magnetic resonance spectroscopy and spectroscopic imaging MRS(I) allow non-invasive, spatially resolved in vivo investigation of specific metabolites, without the use of radioactive tracers. Main body 1 H-MRS(I) is one of the most widely utilized techniques due to its accessibility, while heteronuclear approaches, including 2 H-, 13 C-, 15 N-, and 17 O-MRS(I), broaden MRS(I)'s utility by expanding the scope of accessible metabolites. Technical and methodological advances in nuclear spin hyperpolarization-enhanced MRI further improve signal-to-noise ratio, enabling in vivo detection of low-abundance metabolites. Furthermore, revival of 2 H-MRS(I) has opened new avenues for dynamic metabolic investigation without hyperpolarization. In this review, we provide a conceptual framework for transitioning from a static to a dynamic MRS(I) approach and discuss key considerations for tracer selection, nuclear spin hyperpolarization methods, acquisition hardware, reconstruction, preprocessing, and metabolic modeling. We outline major methodological and translational challenges, including low signal-to-noise ratio, field strength, and vendor hardware variability, as well as a lack of standardization across acquisition, reconstruction, preprocessing, and modeling strategies. Conclusion Dynamic MRS(I) provides a promising foundation for in vivo brain metabolism investigation in NDDs, offering mechanistic insights into metabolic fluxes, reprogramming, and bottlenecks. Although dynamic MRS(I) is limited to a few research institutions, ongoing technical and methodological advances are improving its feasibility, biochemical specificity, and broader implementation. Standardized and harmonized acquisition, reconstruction, and preprocessing protocols are necessary to enable broad clinical implementation of these approaches. Nevertheless, the shift from static to dynamic MRS(I) has great potential to advance biomarker and diagnostic tool development, patient stratification, and longitudinal disease monitoring in NDDs, provided that current challenges and limitations are sufficiently addressed.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Imaging Technologies in Orthodontic Assessment, Referral and Care Pathways: A Scoping Review
abstract: Abstract* Background Artificial intelligence (AI), integrated with imaging technologies, is increasingly applied across orthodontic assessment and care pathways. However, the evidence remains scattered across imaging modalities, clinical applications, AI methodologies, and stages of clinical translation. Methods A scoping review was conducted in accordance with the Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and reported in line with the PRISMA-ScR guidelines. PubMed, Scopus, and IEEE Xplore were searched for studies published between January 2016 and June 2026, with searches supplemented by Google Scholar, OpenAlex, grey literature sources, and citation searching. Eligible studies were mapped descriptively and synthesised thematically using Braun and Clarke’s framework. Results Fifty-four studies were included. AI applications used intraoral and facial photographs, cephalometric radiographs, CBCT, intraoral scans, three-dimensional dental models, and multimodal imaging. Applications ranged from landmark localisation, segmentation, and malocclusion classification to treatment-need assessment, screening, referral support, treatment planning, and remote monitoring. Evidence was strongest for bounded, anatomically verifiable image-analysis tasks, whereas applications involving referral, triage, treatment-need decisions, longitudinal prediction, and workflow integration were less mature. Common limitations included retrospective, single-centre designs; heterogeneous reference standards; limited external validation; inconsistent reporting of calibration and uncertainty; and insufficient evaluation of patient-centred, equity, and service-level outcomes. Conclusions Imaging-based AI in orthodontics has evolved from automated image interpretation to clinician-assisted decision support across the care pathway. Current evidence most strongly supports AI for structured image-analysis tasks, but does not yet support autonomous referral, triage, or treatment-planning decisions. Future research should prioritise prospective multicentre validation, transparent reporting, explainability, fairness, uncertainty handling, and workflow-integrated evaluation to enable safe and clinically useful implementation.

title: Artificial Intelligence for Medical Image Analysis in Low-Resource Settings
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) for medical image analysis is increasingly being developed for low-resource settings, where specialist expertise, imaging equipment, labelled data, and computing resources may be limited. We systematically reviewed 189 studies published between January 2021 and January 2026 to examine how these constraints relate to imaging modalities, clinical applications, and AI methods in low-resource settings. Each study was also assessed against 15 criteria adapted from the FUTURE-AI principles for trustworthy AI. Shortages of clinical expertise were the most common constraint, and portable or lower-cost imaging was widely used. Transfer learning was the most frequent technical strategy (59%), followed by data augmentation (54%) and efficient model design (36%). Medical-image pretraining and self-supervised learning were each used in 4% of studies, and model compression in 3%. Applications were concentrated in retinal disease, pulmonary disease, antenatal care, parasitic diseases, and cervical screening. Beyond these technical and clinical patterns, the trustworthy AI assessment showed a clear gap between documenting how systems were developed and demonstrating how they performed under relevant local conditions. Subgroup performance was evaluated in 24% of studies, intended users or realistic working conditions in 25%, and model explanations with intended users in 4%. Consistent with this gap, among 15 studies that reported the same model and metric during development and in the local setting, 12 performed worse locally. Future research should prioritise representative local evaluation, intended-user assessment, demonstrated resource suitability, and reproducible research practices.

title: Most Colon Grading Mistakes Are Neighbors: Adjacent-Grade Error Shares and Grade-3 Recall on Public Histopathology Embeddings
abstract: Colon histology computer-aided diagnosis (CAD) papers often lead with pooled grading accuracy. That number mixes easy majority-class hits with minority-class misses and treats a Grade 1↔Grade 2 swap as interchangeable with calling poorly differentiated cancer well differentiated. This preprint recomputes stratified five-fold support-vector grading on 560 public colorectal cancer patches with frozen ResNet50 embeddings (Grade 1 n=251, Grade 2 n=210, Grade 3 n=99). Cross-validated accuracy is 73.6% ± 2.9% and macro-F1 is 0.705, but Grade 3 recall is only 0.475. Of 148 residual mistakes, 119 (80.4%) are adjacent-grade swaps; 29 (19.6%) jump from Grade 3 to Grade 1. A published soft-voting ensemble confusion matrix shows the same structure: 86.0% of errors remain adjacent. We treat that adjacent share as the checkable claim—not a new leaderboard—and argue that Grade 3 recall and adjacent versus non-adjacent error counts should be reported before pooled accuracy is read as a deployment summary. Embedding protocol and ensemble confusion-matrix anchors follow a published two-stage colon pipeline; no new patients were enrolled.

title: Pseudoangina as an Unusual Presentation of Non-Osseous Arterial Thoracic Outlet Syndrome: A Case Report.
abstract: Abstract Background Thoracic outlet syndrome (TOS) encompasses disorders caused by compression of the neurovascular structures traversing the thoracic outlet. Arterial thoracic outlet syndrome (aTOS) is the rarest subtype, accounting for approximately 1% of cases. It is typically associated with cervical ribs or other osseous abnormalities and carries a significant risk of distal embolization and limb-threatening ischemia. Presentation with recurrent angina-like chest pain is uncommon and may result in diagnostic delay. Case Presentation A 27-year-old previously healthy man presented with recurrent left-sided chest pain radiating to the neck and left upper limb for four weeks. Initial investigations for a cardiac cause, including serial electrocardiograms, cardiac biomarkers, transthoracic echocardiography, treadmill stress testing, coronary angiography, and Holter monitoring, were normal. Further evaluation revealed intermittent left upper-limb paresthesia and cold intolerance. The Adson maneuver reproduced symptoms and was associated with attenuation of the left radial pulse and dusky discoloration of the fingers. Chest and cervical spine radiographs showed no cervical rib or other osseous abnormality. Dynamic computed tomography angiography demonstrated positional compression of the left subclavian artery during arm abduction, which resolved in the neutral position, while dynamic venography was normal. A diagnosis of left-sided non-osseous arterial thoracic outlet syndrome was established. The patient was referred for vascular surgical evaluation and thoracic outlet decompression. Conclusion Arterial thoracic outlet syndrome should be considered in young patients with recurrent non-cardiac chest pain, particularly when accompanied by upper-limb neurovascular symptoms. A high index of suspicion and dynamic vascular imaging are critical for timely diagnosis, especially in the absence of the osseous abnormalities classically associated with aTOS.

title: Connectome and Depression: Towards Precision Psychiatry Based on Brain Networks
abstract: In recent decades, the study of the human connectome —the comprehensive map of the brain's neural connections— has redefined our understanding of Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) as a spectrum of functional and structural alterations in specific brain networks. This review explores evidence on functional connectivity patterns in MDD, highlighting the involvement of networks such as the default mode network (DMN), frontoparietal network (FPN), salience network (SN), and reward circuits. We analyze patterns detected using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and their potential as biomarkers to predict treatment response to interventions currently included in clinical guidelines and widely used in practice, such as psychotherapy, first-line antidepressants (SSRIs), transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), electroconvulsive therapy (ECT), and sub-anesthetic doses of ketamine. For this purpose, we conducted an integrative narrative review of the scientific literature, selecting articles based on clinical relevance and methodological quality (GRADE), including meta-analyses, systematic reviews, and randomized controlled trials. These findings may contribute to a paradigm shift toward precision psychiatry, increasingly centered on the individual. Although methodological challenges persist that limit their clinical application, understanding the connectome and its relationship with MDD pathogenesis is a fundamental step toward truly personalized mental healthcare.

title: UniMedSeg: Unified Multi-Modal Medical Image Segmentation via Uncertainty-Guided Encoding and Frequency-Spatial Dual-Prompt Decoding
abstract: ABSTRACT Text-driven medical image segmentation demands unified models based on multi-modal learning, capable of processing diverse imaging modalities while providing spatially reliable prediction estimates for clinical practice. Nevertheless, existing vision-language model solutions suffer from poor domain generalization and exhibit limited capability for uncertainty estimation to model the cumulative unreliability of cross-modal alignment across network layers. In this paper, we propose UniMedSeg, a unified vision-language framework for multi-modal medical image segmentation built upon frozen pre-trained vision-language backbones. Our framework incorporates modality-aware adaptation, cross-layer uncertainty-guided encoding, and a frequency-spatial dual-prompt decoder, wherein the progressive uncertainty propagation mechanism of the encoder suppresses misleading cross-modal features, whereas the decoder disentangles anatomical structure and boundary details in the frequency domain under dual textual prompts. Auxiliary losses further sharpen boundary representations and calibrate pixel-wise uncertainty maps. Extensive experiments demonstrate that UniMedSeg preserves competitive in-domain segmentation performance, improves domain generalization, and yields clinically useful spatial risk estimation. The source code is available at https://github.com/699zjl/UniMedSeg . Highlights We propose UniMedSeg , a unified vision-language model for five-modality medical segmentation that outputs segmentation masks and clinical-oriented pixel-level uncertainty maps. A cross-layer uncertainty propagation mechanism is designed to dynamically suppress unreliable vision-language alignment by recursively accumulating historical reliability signals. A frequency-spatial dual-prompt decoder disentangles anatomical structure and boundary details via FFT-based separation and branch-specific text-guided attention to reduce frequency-domain artifacts. Auxiliary boundary contrastive and uncertainty calibration objectives enhance boundary discrimination and enforce consistency between predicted uncertainty and segmentation errors. Extensive experiments on multi-modal medical datasets verify that UniMedSeg yields competitive in-domain performance and favorable out-of-distribution generalization capability.

title: A Case of Primary Leiomyoma of the Chest Wall Showing High Uptake on FDG-PET.
abstract: Introduction Primary leiomyoma of the chest wall is a rare entity. We report a case of primary chest wall leiomyoma with intense uptake on fluorodeoxyglucose PET (FDG-PET), requiring differentiation from malignancy. Case presentation An 82-year-old man with a history of asbestos exposure underwent annual chest CT surveillance. A 19-mm nodule was newly identified on the right chest wall and had not been present on CT the previous year. Although the lesion had well-defined margins on CT, FDG-PET demonstrated intense uptake with a maximum standardized uptake value of 11.8, raising suspicion for malignancy. Surgical resection was performed for diagnostic and therapeutic purposes. Histopathological examination revealed fascicular proliferation of spindle-shaped cells. Immunohistochemical analysis suggested a smooth muscle tumor, and retention of BRCA1-associated protein 1 and methylthioadenosine phosphorylase excluded mesothelioma. Based on these findings, the tumor was diagnosed as a primary leiomyoma of the chest wall. Conclusions Primary leiomyomas of the chest wall are rare and may show high FDG uptake on PET imaging, making differentiation from malignant tumors challenging. A comprehensive evaluation incorporating imaging, intraoperative findings, and pathological assessment is essential for accurate diagnosis.

Based on these findings, the tumor was diagnosed as a primary leiomyoma of the chest wall.

Conclusions

Primary leiomyomas of the chest wall are rare and may show high FDG uptake on PET imaging, making differentiation from malignant tumors challenging. A comprehensive evaluation incorporating imaging, intraoperative findings, and pathological assessment is essential for accurate diagnosis.

title: Learning Features, Not Layouts: Feature-Axis Attention as a Transfer Prior for Medical Imaging
abstract: Natural-image-pretrained foundation models are increasingly adapted to medical imaging, yet transfer remains unreliable under domain shift, modality heterogeneity, and label scarcity. We trace part of this fragility to an overlooked design choice. Standard vision transformers place all global modeling on self-attention over spatial tokens, an object-layout prior well suited to natural scenes but not to medical images, where the discriminative signal lies in feature correlations and texture that recur across scanners while layout does not. We ask whether the axis of global attention, spatial versus feature, is itself a lever for transferable medical representations. Existing channel-aware hybrids confound this question, adding channel attention to a spatially-mixed backbone and leaving the axes coupled and the feature axis unmeasurable in isolation. We design FAD-ViT, a backbone that strictly decouples the two axes, making feature-axis attention the primary global operator and the attention axis a controlled variable. Evaluating comprehensively across 23 classification, segmentation, and low-data tasks under matched tokenization, capacity, and protocol, we find that shifting global attention from the spatial to the feature axis leaves from-scratch performance essentially unchanged, yet markedly strengthens transfer. Identical ImageNet pretraining yields up to roughly three times the transfer gain, with consistent improvements on every held-out segmentation task at up to a quarter the parameter count and far lower compute than standard and channel-attention baselines. The advantage is largest where texture rather than geometry is discriminative, tracking greater reuse of pretrained features. The axis of global attention is thus a design lever for medical transfer, and making it channel-primary is a simple, cheap, and principled choice.

title: Dataset-Specific Encoding of Image Content Underlies Cross-Dataset Failure in Brain MRI Foundation Models
abstract: Frozen features of brain MRI foundation models lose accuracy on new datasets, a failure usually blamed on the features encoding where each scan came from. We show that the failure lies elsewhere. Across 17 public datasets and eight frozen representations, every representation recognizes the MRI sequence within each dataset, yet most fail on an unseen one. The cause is neither dataset encoding nor a shift of each dataset: the content itself is encoded along different directions in each dataset. This explains which datasets fail, for the sequence and for sex, and why removing the dataset signal with INLP, LEACE, CORAL or adversarial training never improves sequence transfer. Only the broadly pretrained 3DINO and SAM-Med3D encode the sequence consistently enough to transfer; the brain-specific BrainIAC and BrainFM do no better than an untrained network. Code is available at https://github.com/BrainFM/brainfm-profiler/tree/main/representation_utility.

title: A4-MR: Abnormality-aware Anatomical Alignment for MR
abstract: Recent advances in large-scale foundation models have enabled strong generalization across a wide range of clinical and research tasks in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). However, existing vision-language MRI models remain limited in anatomy-specific localization and pathology-aware representation, particularly in real-world settings. We introduce A4-MR, a 3D vision-language foundation model trained on approximately 50,000 MRI studies comprising 491,000 series, roughly half of which are paired with radiology reports. A4-MR is designed to: (1) learn anatomy localization through large-scale pretraining with noisy labels; (2) align image and text representations at the anatomical level; and (3) learn distinct representations of healthy and abnormal anatomy. Across a diverse set of downstream tasks, A4-MR outperforms existing foundation models, including a +1.7 AUROC improvement over MedSigLIP for abnormality detection. Using a frozen encoder, A4-MR also surpasses an end-to-end task-specific MedNeXt model for knee segmentation by +1.4 Dice and performs comparably to the best task-specific model for abdominal organ segmentation on AMOS, within 0.4 Dice. Finally, without anatomical prompts, A4-MR localizes 3D anatomy comparably to MedSAM2 provided with ground-truth bounding boxes. Together, these results demonstrate that anatomy-level multimodal alignment and abnormality-aware representation learning can enable a single MRI foundation model to support localization, segmentation, and pathology-related tasks.

title: CliQ-RRG: Clinical-Knowledge Guided Disease-aware Visual-Textual Alignment for QA-Style Radiology Report Generation
abstract: Radiology reports are essential for diagnostic reasoning and patient care, yet their manual preparation is time-consuming and cognitively demanding. Automatic radiology report generation (RRG) offers a scalable alternative, but existing models often produce lengthy, unstructured narratives that overlook diagnostic cues and multi-view information. We present Clinical-Knowledge Guided Disease-aware Visual-Textual Alignment for QA-Style Radiology Report Generation (CliQ-RRG), a unified two-stage framework for interpretable and clinically grounded reporting. In Stage 1, CliQ-RRG employs a Disease-aware Visual-Textual Alignment module that aligns image and text representations using predicted disease embeddings, reinforced by a Prior-Guided Attention Module (PrAM) to capture multi-view dependencies across current and prior scans. In Stage 2, GraphRAG-guided retrieval augments intermediate textual representations with graph-grounded clinical evidence, and a large language model restructures them into concise, interpretable question-answer (QA) pairs with diagnostic summaries. Experiments on two public chest X-ray benchmarks demonstrate that CliQ-RRG consistently outperforms prior methods across both lexical and clinical metrics, generating accurate and clinically coherent QA-style radiology reports. Code is available at: https://github.com/chandravardhan-singh-raghaw/CliQ-RRG.

title: Stochastic Finite-Transition Learning and Exploration for Accelerated MRI Reconstruction
abstract: Generative MRI reconstruction maps an initial source distribution to the target image distribution along a learned recovery trajectory. Common generative methods, such as diffusion and flow, typically learn fine-grained local dynamics whose integration defines this global mapping, hence requiring many network evaluations at inference. Existing few-step sampling approaches can lower computational burden by approximating large transformations from local dynamics, albeit at the expense of reconstruction fidelity. FLEX-MRI instead partitions recovery into a small number of finite intervals between retained states defined by progressive changes in k-space support, and directly learns the reconstruction change across each interval. Because such finite transitions can admit multiple plausible outcomes, FLEX-MRI combines support-relaxed finite-transition learning with stochastic exploration. During training, randomized k-space sampling masks define finite-transition targets with varying support, while the prediction loss remains unrestricted by each individual mask. At inference, FLEX-MRI perturbs a random subset of currently estimated k-space coefficients, allowing the learned predictor to stochastically explore alternative transition paths. Each predicted state is then reconciled with the acquired measurements through data consistency. We theoretically show that this stochastic exploration induces nonzero transition-level variation through the learned recovery map and data consistency without requiring an auxiliary generative sampler. Experiments on multi-coil MRI datasets show that FLEX-MRI outperforms competing methods while maintaining computational efficiency comparable to few-step baselines.

title: The Predictability Bias of Joint-Embedding Predictive Learning in Medical Imaging
abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) learn by predicting teacher representations of masked regions from visible context. Point prediction summarizes the conditional target distribution and cannot reproduce variation that the context does not resolve. We call this constraint predictability bias. In computed tomography (CT), recurrent anatomy is predictable from context, whereas the sporadic, localized pathology that determines clinical interpretation often is not. We introduce TAP-JEPA, a ViT-B/3D trained on 113,611 CT volumes that is competitive with state-of-the-art encoders (COLIPRI, Merlin, VoxelFM) in scan-level classification. We then audit the learned predictive pathway by replaying the exact masking, teacher, and predictor computations used during training. Prediction lowers the mean Skill (prevalence-normalized average precision) from 0.388 to 0.271 for pathology, but only from 0.921 to 0.873 for anatomy. Along the teacher direction, separating pathology from matched control regions in the same organ, prediction moves pathology 34.7% toward the controls and controls 13.6% toward pathology, with larger shifts farther from visible context. Replacing visible matched-control representations increases surrounding-target prediction loss more than fully replacing pathology representations across four pathology categories. Downstream, removing all final-layer pathology tokens reduces the decision margin by at most 0.45% in four of seven scan-level probes. Together, these results show that contextual predictability is not a sufficient proxy for clinical relevance in medical representation learning. Training objectives should therefore retain diagnostic features regardless of their predictability from surrounding anatomy.

title: Radiomics-Based Thyroid Nodule Classification with Label-Conditional Conformal Prediction
abstract: Thyroid nodule malignancy assessment relies on ultrasound imaging, yet current risk stratification systems suffer from substantial interobserver variability, contributing to a high rate of unnecessary biopsies. We propose a radiomics-based framework combining quantitative feature extraction via PyRadiomics with a Generalized Additive Model (GAM) classifier, selected among six candidates for its favorable trade-off between discriminative performance and interpretability. To complement point predictions with uncertainty estimates, Cross-Conformal Prediction with label-conditional guarantees is applied, flagging ambiguous cases for clinical review rather than forcing a binary decision. Experiments are conducted on TN5000, a publicly available ultrasound dataset of thyroid nodules. After Spearman correlation filtering, 36 features are retained and the GAM achieves an AUC of $0.89$, a sensitivity of $0.83$, and a specificity of $0.82$ on the validation set. At a significance level $ε=0.09$, selected to ensure empirical coverage guarantees on both classes, 63\% of nodules on the test set receive a certain (i.e., single-label) prediction, with conditional precision of $0.94$ for certain malignant and conditional Negative Predictive Value (NPV) of $0.73$ for certain benign cases, while the remaining 37\% are referred to the clinician.

title: SADL: A Size-Adaptive Decision Layer for Chronic Stroke Lesion Segmentation in ISLES 2026
abstract: Chronic ischemic stroke lesions are difficult to segment on T1-weighted MRI. Their appearance overlaps with healthy tissue, and their volumes span four orders of magnitude, so voxel-level and lesion level metrics often disagree. We build an eleven-member nnU-Net ensemble that covers five design axes: a baseline dice + top-K loss, heavy augmentation, per-lesion volume loss re-weighting, stochastic weight averaging, and a sampling-and-architecture block that pairs cohort-balanced sampling with a residual-encoder backbone. Weighted soft-map fusion of the members feeds a tuned decision layer, SADL, that estimates lesion volume, applies an adaptive per-lesion-size threshold, prunes components by voxel count and peak probability, and adds a never-empty rescue. All fusion weights and per-bucket parameters are fitted on out-of-fold (OOF) predictions, so tuning never touches the held-out test set. On a site-disjoint 91-case holdout, SADL reaches Dice 0.7322, lesion-F1 0.7461 and PR-AUC 0.8430 when scored online with the challenge's released evaluation code. A paired non-parametric bootstrap against a reference single ensemble member confirms the lesion-F1 gain at p=0.024, and the gain is largest in the small-lesion regime, where the rescue step recovers cases that a fixed threshold would silently discard.

title: EchoTab: Learning Measurement-Grounded Representations for Echocardiographic Diagnosis through Tabular Reconstruction
abstract: Diagnostic information in multi-view medical imaging studies, like echocardiography, is distributed across views, each capturing different aspects of cardiac structure and function. In clinical practice, these views are first interpreted through quantitative measurements, which then support specific diagnoses. However, existing echo representation learning methods do not explicitly model measurements as an intermediate representation between views and diagnosis. As a result, individual measurements are not explicitly represented in a form that downstream diagnostic tasks can selectively use, hindering accurate diagnosis. Inspired by this hierarchical clinical workflow, we introduce EchoTab, a measurement-grounded representation learning framework that represents multi-view echocardiography studies using measurement-specific tokens as an intermediate representation between echo views and diagnosis. Each measurement token selectively attends to the views relevant to its estimation and is trained through tabular reconstruction to predict the corresponding measurement value. The resulting tokens form a factorized echo representation, which encode clinically meaningful structural and functional properties and can be selectively used for downstream diagnosis. Unlike the commonly used contrastive approaches, EchoTab does not require negative samples or large batch sizes. Experiments on two datasets demonstrate that EchoTab learns effective measurement-grounded representations that improve diagnosis classification in multi-view echocardiography and its learned attention aligns with established measurement-view relationships used by cardiologists. Our code is accessible at https://github.com/michelleespranita/EchoTab.

title: Thyroid Nodule Segmentation in Ultrasound Images with Conformal Uncertainty Estimation
abstract: Thyroid nodules affect a large proportion of the general population. Although most are benign, a non-negligible fraction is malignant. Ultrasound imaging is the primary diagnostic modality, and accurate nodule segmentation is a prerequisite for CAD systems to classify malignancy and assess metastatic risk.\\ In this work, we propose a thyroid nodule segmentation framework that integrates a DeepLabV3+, channel-attention modules and post-hoc conformal prediction, providing both accurate mask and pixel-level uncertainty estimates. We address thyroid ultrasound nodule segmentation as the first stage of a pipeline that also includes malignancy classification and metastatic risk prediction. We adopt DeepLabV3+, whose Atrous Spatial Pyramid Pooling (ASPP) captures multi-scale context, with an EfficientNet-B5 backbone for its accuracy-efficiency trade-off. Additionally, we test three channel-attention modules: Squeeze-and-Excitation, CBAM and Grouped Channel Attention (GCA), paired with two loss formulations (Dice-BCE and Boundary).\\ Since binary masks do not indicate prediction confidence, we wrap the trained model with a split conformal prediction layer that produces pixel-level uncertainty maps with statistical coverage guarantees.\\ We evaluate all configurations on the TN3K public benchmark using a fixed split and directly compare them with state-of-the-art methods. The plain backbone already improves upon previously reported results, with CBAM + Dice-BCE emerging as the best overall configuration.

The plain backbone already improves upon previously reported results, with CBAM + Dice-BCE emerging as the best overall configuration.

title: Open-H-RF: A Large-Scale Ultrasound Raw Channel Dataset Initiative
abstract: Medical ultrasound is a widely accessible, real-time imaging modality, yet progress in data-driven ultrasound research is constrained by the scarcity of large, open collections of raw channel data. Existing public datasets are predominantly based on reconstructed images, while the smaller number of open raw channel datasets is generally specialized to individual reconstruction or imaging tasks, limiting the development of general-purpose methods and foundation models that operate directly on ultrasound signals. While interpretive tasks can be performed on reconstructed images, many of the key technical challenges in ultrasound imaging, such as aberration correction and reverberation reduction, require the raw channel data itself. We introduce Open-H-RF, a community-driven open dataset initiative comprising approximately 40 TB of medical ultrasound raw channel data in 19,332 acquisitions, contributed by 38 institutions across academia and industry, spanning in-vivo, phantom, and simulated data. Each dataset is annotated with a number of supported tasks, ranging from generalized reconstruction, speed-of-sound estimation, and aberration correction to blood flow imaging, motion estimation, quantitative ultrasound, and image interpretation. Open-H-RF provides a unified, self-contained data format that captures raw channel data together with the acquisition, probe, metadata, and reconstruction information required for reproducible processing across scanners and acquisition schemes. The corpus is publicly hosted under a permissive CC BY 4.0 license and can be streamed programmatically and selectively at scale. By bringing heterogeneous ultrasound data into a common representation, backed by modern data infrastructure, Open-H-RF lowers the barrier to working with raw channel data and aims to open medical ultrasound research to new communities. See https://open-h.github.io/Open-H-RF.

title: Can machines reason non-verbally?
abstract: Modern machines can solve equations, follow logic and reason through language, yet they still struggle with problems that require visual non-verbal reasoning. This is evident even in advanced systems such as DeepSeek, ChatGPT and Gemini, which remain limited on visual tasks such as completing abstract patterns or delineating ambiguous regions-of-interest. Unlike explicit intermediate steps in verbal reasoning which can be verified through logic or automated tests, visual reasoning involves implicit intermediate steps with no clear methods for verification. Non-verbal reasoning is therefore challenging to model and, as a result, remains a fundamental limitation of current machine intelligence. Here we introduce GenVerOpt, a general framework that unifies generation, verification and optimisation into a reasoning pipeline for machines. By generating candidate solutions, verifying their correctness, and iteratively refining them, GenVerOpt enables per-sample optimisation rather than relying solely on dataset-level trends captured during model training. This process mirrors human problem-solving where multiple possibilities are imagined, evaluated, and refined until a correct solution emerges. Across diverse domains, GenVerOpt demonstrates capabilities beyond existing systems: it surpasses humans on abstract IQ puzzles, matches clinicians in prostate cancer segmentation, exceeds experts in liver vessel reconstruction and outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in tumour boundary alignment. These results show that machine reasoning can extend beyond language, establishing visual non-verbal reasoning as a foundation for more flexible and generalisable intelligence.

title: Exploring the Latent Structure of AMD Severity Using Retinal Foundation Models
abstract: Retinal foundation models have demonstrated strong performance across a wide range of ophthalmic tasks, yet relatively little is known about how disease-related information is represented within their learned embeddings and whether this distribution influences downstream prediction performance. In this work, we use Age-related Macular Degeneration (AMD) as a case study to investigate how disease severity is represented within the embedding space of RET-CLIP, a retinal vision-language foundation model, using bilateral fundus images from the AREDS dataset, benchmarked against non-retinal encoders. We first characterize the distribution of AMD severity within the learned representation space and then evaluate how this structure influences classification performance across three clinically relevant task formulations of increasing granularity. Finally, we analyze the most influential latent dimensions combining feature attribution, statistical phenotype association, and qualitative image analyses. Our results show that RET-CLIP represents AMD severity as a continuous spectrum rather than a set of discrete categories, with healthy and advanced disease stages exhibiting clearer separation than intermediate ones. This organization was reflected in downstream performance, which decreased from a balanced accuracy of 0.844 and 0.814 for binary AMD and Late-AMD detection respectively to 0.446 for six-class grading. Furthermore, the most influential latent dimensions were statistically associated to distinct retinal phenotypes, including drusen accumulation, pigmentary alterations, and advanced retinal lesions. These findings suggest that the structure of retinal foundation-model representations influences the difficulty of clinically relevant prediction tasks and demonstrate the potential of representation-level analysis for understanding disease organization and improving interpretability.

title: C$^2$LUE: Clinically Aligned Patient-Level Ultrasound Diagnosis via Evidence-Aware Multi-Instance Learning
abstract: Patient-level ultrasound diagnosis demands not only high predictive accuracy but also clinically aligned mitigation of asymmetric diagnostic risks. While Multi-Instance Learning (MIL) effectively models routine multi-view exams, standard aggregators often dilute heterogeneous diagnostic cues and optimize solely for global accuracy. This frequently yields undesirable sensitivity-specificity trade-offs. To bridge this gap, we propose C$^2$LUE, a novel MIL framework coupling evidence aware aggregation with risk-aligned regularization. To preserve evidence heterogeneity and prevent unimodal attention collapse, C$^2$LUE employs a multi-query cross-attention mechanism built upon a LoRA-adapted DINOv3 backbone. Multiple latent queries explicitly extract and disentangle diverse morphological patterns from the ultrasound sequence. Furthermore, to improve clinical risk alignment, we introduce a dynamic trade-off regularization objective that penalizes sensitivity-specificity imbalance during training. Rather than leaving the clinical trade-off entirely to post-hoc threshold adjustment, this objective encourages the learned score distribution toward a more balanced operating region. Extensive evaluations on patient-level, biopsy-proven thyroid and breast ultrasound datasets demonstrate that C$^2$LUE consistently outperforms prior alternatives. By uniting strong discrimination with a balanced error profile, C$^2$LUE provides a promising solution for real-world ultrasound screening and diagnosis.

title: CAPTOR: a vision-language foundation model for Chest-Abdomen-Pelvis Oncologic CT
abstract: Purpose : To develop and evaluate CAPTOR, a deep-learning vision-language foundation model for oncologic chest-abdomen-pelvis (CAP) CT interpretation. Materials & Methods : CAPTOR (Chest-Abdomen-Pelvis foundaTion model for Oncologic Radiology) is a contrastive vision-language model, trained using a pretraining strategy for oncologic CAP CT (in single- or multiple-series acquisitions), on a multicenter retrospective dataset from North America, Europe and Asia, predominantly from tumor lesion examinations. CAPTOR was compared with state-of-the-art CT foundation models on three downstream tasks: disease detection, survival prediction using TumorImagingBench and image retrieval. Classification and retrieval were both evaluated on held-out internal and public test sets, stratified by anatomical coverage and indication. Bootstrap resampling was used to estimate confidence intervals, and pairwise comparisons were performed using permutation tests. Results : CAPTOR was trained and tested on 25,512 and 10,794 CT-report pairs respectively. TumorImagingBench datasets comprised between 134 and 421 studies each. CAPTOR outperformed all baseline models, on the classification task, on the CAP subset (AUC 0.767, 95%CI: 0.734-0.793, vs. 0.695, 95%CI: 0.645-0.736 for the next-best, p<0.001) and oncologic subset (AUC 0.784, 95%CI: 0.759-0.805, vs. 0.734, 95%CI: 0.703-0.767 p<0.001), ranked first on three of the four oncologic prognostic benchmarks, and achieved superior retrieval performance on CAP and oncologic subsets. Conclusion : A foundation model trained on oncology-enriched CAP CT data outperformed relevant state-of-the-art models in its target clinical context, underscoring the importance of clinically aligned pretraining. We release our preprocessing, training and inference code : https://github.com/Guerbet-AI/CAPTOR and model weights : https://huggingface.co/Guerbet-AI/CAPTOR

title: BigCell: Generating Gigapixel Whole-Slide Images
abstract: Whole-slide images (WSIs) are gigapixel-scale digital scans of histopathology tissue and serve as the primary basis for cancer diagnosis. Existing histopathology generative models operate at the patch scale, producing fixed-size tiles of at most 1024$\times$1024 pixels which encompass only a small fraction of the WSI. In contrast, text reports for clinical diagnoses and slide-level diagnostic labels -- the supervision that exists at scale -- operate at the whole-slide level. We present BigCell, the first approach to generate coherent whole-slide histopathology images at native gigapixel resolution. BigCell trains a flow-matching transformer at 2048$\times$2048 pixels on over 120,000 publicly available WSIs spanning multiple organ types. Conditioning on embeddings from pathology foundation models and using an inference-time sliding-window pipeline, BigCell generates coherent images of up to 32,768$\times$32,768 pixels, outperforming prior tile generators on both tile-level and slide-level fidelity metrics. To make gigapixel synthesis practical, we introduce an adaptive scheduling strategy that prioritizes important slide regions, speeding up image generation by over 3\ttimes with minimal quality degradation. Furthermore, we propose the first text-to-image synthesis at 8k resolution by training a separate model that produces dense conditioning grids directly from pathology text reports. We demonstrate that augmenting with synthetic samples improves slide-level few-shot classification performance by up to $18 \%$ over baselines trained on real data.

title: Artificial Intelligence Models Based on Medical Imaging Achieve Accurate Detection of Rotator Cuff Tear and Initial Predictive Capability for Postoperative Outcomes: A Systematic Review.
abstract: Purpose To assess the performance of artificial intelligence (AI) compared with physicians in detecting rotator cuff tear (RCT) on medical imaging and evaluating the ability of AI to predict outcomes after arthroscopic rotator cuff repair. Methods A comprehensive search was conducted in the PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Cochrane Library databases from their inception to July 15, 2025. The criteria were as follows: (1) original studies employing AI to detect RCT or predict outcomes after arthroscopic rotator cuff repair and (2) case reports, reviews, and editorials were excluded. This review followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines and was registered on the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews. Results A total of 37 studies met the inclusion and exclusion criteria, encompassing 46,593 patients. The mean age of the patients was 55.8 years, with an average female representation of 52.2%. AI models developed for diagnosing RCT using magnetic resonance imaging, ultrasound, and radiographic images showed excellent performance, achieving average area under the curves and accuracies of 89.5% and 0.93, 91% and 0.97, and 84% and 0.86, respectively. AI models using radiographs and magnetic resonance imaging have shown performance in diagnosing RCT that surpasses that of junior clinicians, with magnetic resonance imaging-based models performing at a level comparable to senior clinicians. AI models developed to predict retear after arthroscopic rotator cuff repair showed an average accuracy of 83.4% and an area under the curve of 0.83. Older and women were the most common risk factors for postoperative retear identified in the included studies. Conclusions AI models significantly improved diagnostic accuracy based on medical imaging and showed promising predictive performance, particularly regarding rotator cuff retear. However, predictions related to functional scores exhibited relatively lower accuracy. Level of evidence Level III, systematic review of Level II and III studies.

title: The Arthroscopic Wafer Procedure Provides Successful Midterm Outcomes for Idiopathic Ulnar Impaction Syndrome: A Minimum 5-Year Follow-Up.
abstract: Purpose To evaluate the midterm clinical and radiologic outcomes of the arthroscopic wafer procedure for idiopathic ulnar impaction syndrome with a minimum 5-year follow-up. Methods Patients with idiopathic ulnar impaction syndrome and less than 4 mm of positive ulnar variance who underwent the arthroscopic wafer procedure between May 2009 and February 2017 were analyzed. Only patients with a minimum follow-up of 5 years were included. Clinical outcomes, including the visual analog scale pain score; Mayo Wrist Score; Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder, and Hand score; grip strength; and range of motion, were assessed. A cohort-specific minimal clinically important difference analysis was performed. Radiographic changes in the distal radioulnar joint (DRUJ) were reviewed, and univariate logistic regression identified prognostic factors for DRUJ changes. Results Forty patients (10 men, 30 women; mean age, 54.0 years; mean follow-up, 73.3 months) were analyzed. Clinical outcomes improved significantly (all P < .001): visual analog scale (5.5-1.7), Mayo Wrist Score (51.9-86.5), Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder, and Hand (47.7-14.3), and grip strength (11.7-15.9 kg). Minimal clinically important difference achievement rates were 100% for visual analog scale, 100% for Mayo Wrist Score, 92.5% for Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder, and Hand, and 55.0% for grip strength. On sex-disaggregated analysis, male patients showed significantly greater grip strength than female patients (19.4 vs 14.7 kg, P = .009), with no other significant differences. One patient required conversion to ulnar shortening osteotomy. No significant complications occurred. Eight patients showed asymptomatic DRUJ arthritis. Preoperative ulnar variance significantly predicted postoperative DRUJ arthritis (odds ratio, 4.393; P = .015). Conclusions The arthroscopic wafer procedure showed favorable midterm outcomes at a minimum 5-year follow-up in appropriately selected patients, with high proportions of patients achieving clinically meaningful improvements. Postoperative radiographic DRUJ arthritis was observed in some patients, who remained asymptomatic, and appeared to be associated with greater preoperative ulnar variance. Level of evidence Level IV, retrospective case series.

title: Acute rather than insidious symptom onset is associated with better postoperative outcomes after transtibial pull-out repair for medial meniscus posterior root tears.
abstract: Purpose To compare clinical and radiologic outcomes after transtibial pull-out repair for medial meniscus posterior root tears (MMPRTs) between patients with acute and insidious symptom onset. Methods Patients who underwent transtibial pull-out repair for MMPRTs between March 2022 and December 2023 and had a minimum 2-year follow-up were retrospectively reviewed. Patients were classified into an acute-onset group, defined by abrupt symptom onset during or immediately after a clear inciting knee incident, or an insidious-onset group, defined by gradually progressive symptoms without a definite precipitating event. Outcomes included patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) and radiologic parameters. PROMs comprised the International Knee Documentation Committee (IKDC) and Lysholm scores, with minimal clinically important difference (MCID) achievement also assessed. Radiologic outcomes included Kellgren-Lawrence (KL) grade progression, meniscal extrusion and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) healing status. Results A total of 49 patients were included (28 acute-onset, 21 insidious-onset). Both groups showed significant improvement in IKDC and Lysholm scores, with similar MCID achievement rates. At final follow-up, the Acute Group had higher median IKDC scores than the Insidious Group (73.0 [66.8-79.0] vs. 67.0 [62.0-69.0]; p = 0.02) and Lysholm scores (76.0 [73.0-78.0] vs. 71.0 [70.0-74.0]; p < 0.01). KL-grade progression was less frequent in the Acute Group (1/28 [3.6%] vs. 8/21 [38.1%]; p < 0.01). Meniscal extrusion was also lower (3.3 [2.9-3.5] vs. 3.9 [3.1-4.0] mm; p = 0.01), although the absolute difference was small. MRI healing status did not differ between groups. Conclusion Acute-onset MMPRTs were associated with better postoperative functional outcomes and less radiologic progression than insidious-onset MMPRTs, although the clinical relevance of the small difference in meniscal extrusion remains uncertain. Therefore, symptom-onset pattern may provide potentially useful information for preoperative prognostic counselling, but this association should be interpreted cautiously and confirmed in prospective studies. Level of evidence Level III.

A total of 49 patients were included (28 acute-onset, 21 insidious-onset). Both groups showed significant improvement in IKDC and Lysholm scores, with similar MCID achievement rates. At final follow-up, the Acute Group had higher median IKDC scores than the Insidious Group (73.0 [66.8-79.0] vs. 67.0 [62.0-69.0]; p = 0.02) and Lysholm scores (76.0 [73.0-78.0] vs. 71.0 [70.0-74.0]; p < 0.01). KL-grade progression was less frequent in the Acute Group (1/28 [3.6%] vs. 8/21 [38.1%]; p < 0.01). Meniscal extrusion was also lower (3.3 [2.9-3.5] vs. 3.9 [3.1-4.0] mm; p = 0.01), although the absolute difference was small. MRI healing status did not differ between groups.

Conclusion

Acute-onset MMPRTs were associated with better postoperative functional outcomes and less radiologic progression than insidious-onset MMPRTs, although the clinical relevance of the small difference in meniscal extrusion remains uncertain. Therefore, symptom-onset pattern may provide potentially useful information for preoperative prognostic counselling, but this association should be interpreted cautiously and confirmed in prospective studies.

Level of evidence

Level III.
